request_context: A request to turn business requirements or product documentation into development-ready agile work items, with epics, user stories and testable acceptance criteria.

rules.source_quote: Acceptance criteria describe implementation details instead of observable behavior
rules.outcome: Acceptance criteria describe what a user or tester can observe happening, and do not prescribe technical implementation such as specific databases, frameworks, endpoints or code structure.
rules.why: Implementation-laden criteria over-specify the solution, constrain the developers and cannot be verified from the user's point of view.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirements for a feature where technical specifics are tempting to include in criteria, such as search, export or notifications.

rules.source_quote: Missing error conditions and edge cases in acceptance criteria
rules.outcome: Acceptance criteria cover failure and boundary situations, such as invalid input, empty results, permission problems or service errors, in addition to the successful path.
rules.why: Stories with only happy-path criteria leave failure behavior undefined and cause rework and defects later.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirements for a feature with user input or external dependencies, such as a payment or upload flow.

rules.source_quote: Stories are too large to complete in one sprint (1-5 days)
rules.outcome: Each story is small enough to be completed by a team within a single sprint, roughly one to five days of work, and large or complex capabilities are split into several stories rather than kept as one.
rules.why: Oversized stories cannot be estimated or finished within an iteration and hide risk.
rules.scenario_hint: A broad requirement such as a complete checkout or reporting module that could be written as one big story.

rules.source_quote: Personas are generic ("user", "admin") instead of specific
rules.outcome: Each story names a specific, meaningful persona with a role and context (for example a particular kind of reviewer or engineer) instead of a bare generic 'user' or 'admin'.
rules.why: Generic personas hide whose need is being met and weaken the value statement.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirements document that mentions only 'users' and 'admins' without further detail.

rules.source_quote: Acceptance criteria use vague terms ("fast", "easy") instead of measurable outcomes
rules.outcome: Acceptance criteria express quality expectations as measurable thresholds, such as a response time in seconds or a number of steps, rather than words like fast, easy or intuitive.
rules.why: Vague wording cannot be tested, so teams disagree about whether a story is done.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirements that say the feature must be fast, simple or user friendly.

rules.source_quote: Separate different filtering, sorting, and display criteria into distinct stories
rules.outcome: Distinct capabilities such as filtering by different attributes, sorting and display options are written as separate stories, each focused on one capability, rather than bundled together.
rules.why: Bundled stories are harder to estimate, test and deliver incrementally.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirement for a list or table view with several filters, sort options and display modes.

rules.source_quote: Stories are not independent (circular dependencies between stories)
rules.outcome: Stories can be built and delivered without circular dependencies on each other, and any real dependency or assumption between stories is called out explicitly.
rules.why: Circular or hidden dependencies block sprint planning and delivery.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirements with tightly coupled features, such as account creation, login and profile management.

rules.outcome: When the source requirements are ambiguous or incomplete, the answer names the specific gaps, states reasonable assumptions, and asks targeted clarifying questions instead of silently inventing details.
rules.why: Silent guesses on missing information produce stories that misrepresent what the business wants.
rules.scenario_hint: A short or vague requirement description lacking details about users, rules or limits.

rules.source_quote: Stories missing performance or scale requirements where applicable
rules.outcome: Where relevant, stories include performance, volume or scale expectations, such as expected load or maximum response time, stated in measurable terms.
rules.why: Omitted non-functional needs surface late as costly defects.
rules.scenario_hint: Requirements for a high-traffic or data-heavy feature such as search over large catalogs.

rules.source_quote: Trace requirements back to their source location in the document for reference
rules.outcome: Stories and epics can be traced back to the section or item of the supplied document or business objective they came from.
rules.why: Without traceability reviewers cannot check that all requirements were covered.
rules.scenario_hint: Any request to convert an uploaded requirements document into stories.

rules.source_quote: MVP produces 10-15 stories for fastest path to value. Production produces 20-30 stories for full feature set. Full scope produces 30-40 stories including edge cases.
rules.outcome: The number of stories matches the requested scope: roughly 10 to 15 for a minimum viable product, 20 to 30 for a production release and 30 to 40 for full scope with edge cases.
rules.why: A story count far off the requested scope gives the team too little or too much work to plan.
rules.scenario_hint: Request that specifies an MVP, production or full scope delivery.

rules.source_quote: User stories follow "As a [persona], I want [action] so that [benefit]" with 3-8 testable acceptance criteria per story.
rules.outcome: Each story has a short title, a one-sentence description naming who wants what and why, in the familiar role-goal-benefit form, and a bulleted list of three to eight acceptance criteria.
rules.scenario_hint: Any request to write user stories from requirements.
